newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey plans fines for media insulting state.
newsitem.headline: Turkey plans fines for media insulting state.

text.p: Turkey's justice minister said on Friday the government, rocked by press reports of ties between the security forces and organised crime, would impose fines on the media for insulting the state.
"Insults, abuse and derision against the government and judiciary are what concern us. New regulations must thus be set in this regard," Sevket Kazan told a news conference.
The largely secularist media has played a key role in probing a car crash scandal linking a top police official, a gangster and an MP from the ruling coalition.
"Public order has been upset, individual rights are being crushed under foot," Kazan, from the Islamist wing of the government, told reporters.

The intense media focus on the scandal prompted a parliamentary debate on Turkey's lively media, which has grown in recent years to around 20 major television stations and about the same number of big daily papers.

Under the new regulations, fines would reflect the circulation and financial position of the offending broadcaster or press organ, Kazan said. Fines would be divided by 10 if the offending article or broadcast was corrected.
Existing laws allow Turkish journalists and writers to be jailed for articles deemed to support Kurdish separatism.
The minister rejected media assertions the government planned a censorship law, saying the regulations would apply only after material was published or broadcast.
Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has been warning the secularist press for months that he will act against what he says is unfair and biased reporting.

Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, a former prime minister and leader of the conservative coalition partner, has often been the target of corruption allegations in the media, which have also linked her to the latest car crash.
The scandal led to the resignation of the interior minister.
